title: History of the Second Larrikin (ಕನ್ನಡ)

full_text:
In the gold souk of Aleppo operated a sly moneychanger named Bahram, who used two sets of brass weights: a slightly heavier set when he bought silver and gold coins from travelers, and a lighter set when he sold them back, cheating both ways.

A clever student named Tariq observed this fraud. He took a hollowed-out brass inkpot, filled it with molten lead until it weighed precisely twelve ounces, and polished it until it gleamed like pure gold bullion.

Tariq walked into Bahram's booth:
'Peace, master of the scale. I have an ingotted ornament of heavy mountain gold. Weigh it for me, and give me silver dirhams in exchange, for I must pay my tuition at the college.'

Bahram's eyes gleamed with greed. He placed Tariq's brass inkpot upon the scale, secretly using his heavy buying weights.
'Aha!' said Bahram, intending to cheat the student. 'My scale shows it weighs only ten ounces. I can pay thee only ten ounces of silver.'

Tariq feigned sorrow: 'Ah, my scale must be mistaken. Very well, give me ten ounces of silver.'
Bahram counted out ten ounces of silver coins using his light selling weights—which in reality weighed only eight ounces!

Tariq took the silver, then turned and shouted to the Market Overseer passing by:
'O Inspector of Weights! Come witness the miracle of Aleppo!'
The Overseer entered the booth with his certified imperial balances.
Tariq declared: 'I offered this merchant a piece of metal which he certified upon his scales as weighing ten ounces of pure gold. Here is the silver he gave me. Let us test his scales and certified weights before your eyes!'

The Overseer weighed both: Bahram's weights were tested against the imperial standards and found blatantly falsified! The Overseer confiscated Bahram's scales, smashed his falsified weights in the public square, and fined him five hundred dinars to be distributed to cheated customers!

Bahram was banned from the moneychanger's guild, while Tariq demonstrated that those who construct traps of false measures inevitably step into their own snares.
moral: Deceitful weights and dishonest balances bring public exposure and ruin to the covetous. [KN]
